one_liner: Did SA-1B swallow the test sets? Measure foundation-training contamination of segmentation benchmarks with near-duplicate forensics.
problem: Foundation models train on web-scale corpora that plausibly contain benchmark test images (or near-duplicates); for segmentation this contamination has never been quantified, though it silently converts zero-shot claims into memorization measurements.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: near-duplicate detection between foundation training sets (SA-1B, LAION-derived) and standard segmentation test sets (COCO, ADE20K, DAVIS) will find nontrivial contamination rates, per-image zero-shot performance is measurably higher on contaminated items (memorization signal), and decontaminated re-scoring shrinks published zero-shot gaps between foundations - benchmark contamination is a live confounder in dense prediction, not just NLP.
why_important: Zero-shot segmentation claims underpin the foundation-model narrative; contamination-corrected numbers are the ones that matter.
why_possibly_novel: Dense-benchmark contamination forensics is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search (NLP contamination studies are KNOWN).
minimal_experiment: Run scalable near-dup detection (embedding + hash) between public shards of SA-1B/LAION and test sets, stratify model performance by contamination status.
main_risk: Only public shards are checkable; report bounds, not point estimates, for closed corpora.

one_liner: Correct the test sets: estimate dense-label error rates on major benchmarks and measure how repairs reorder the leaderboards.
problem: KNOWN: classification test sets contain pervasive label errors (Northcutt et al.). Dense benchmarks likely contain region- and boundary-level errors at higher rates (harder annotation), but error-rate estimates and leaderboard sensitivity to repairs do not exist for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: model-consensus-guided expert re-audit will find pixel-level label fault rates of several percent on major benchmarks (concentrated in occlusion boundaries and class confusions), repairing them changes top-model rankings in a measurable fraction of comparisons, and - critically - the models that gain most from repair are those trained WITHOUT the benchmark's sibling training set (label errors currently favor style-matched models).
why_important: Leaderboards steer the field; if their references are faulty in a direction that favors in-ecosystem models, progress measurement is structurally biased.
why_possibly_novel: Repair-sensitivity analysis of dense leaderboards is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Consensus-flag suspicious regions on 2 benchmarks, expert-adjudicate 3k regions, re-score public models on repaired references.
main_risk: Adjudication of genuinely ambiguous regions; use the three-state protocol (decidable-error vs ambiguous) to keep claims clean.

one_liner: The polygon ceiling: COCO's coarse polygons impose a measurable upper bound on learnable and measurable boundary quality.
problem: COCO masks average few vertices per object; both training signal and evaluation reference inherit this coarseness. The exact ceiling it imposes - on what models can learn and on what evaluation can detect - has not been quantified, though COCO remains the field's central training source.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: comparing COCO polygons against high-fidelity re-annotations will yield a per-size boundary-error floor (the polygon artifact spectrum), models trained on COCO plateau AT this floor (their boundary style measurably mimics polygon geometry - straight-segment artifacts detectable in predictions), and boundary-metric differences between models evaluated on COCO below the floor are meaningless - one number (the ceiling) reframing hundreds of comparisons.
why_important: Establishes when 'better boundaries on COCO' can even be a real claim, and quantifies the training tax of polygon supervision that the ecosystem inherits.
why_possibly_novel: Polygon-artifact ceiling quantification with mimicry detection is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: High-fidelity re-annotation of 500 COCO objects, compute artifact spectra, test for straight-segment mimicry in model predictions, derive the evaluable floor.
main_risk: Re-annotation cost; 500 objects suffice for the spectrum but per-class claims need more.

one_liner: Class definitions drift across dataset versions and papers: 'road' 2016 is not 'road' 2024 - measure semantic versioning debt.
problem: Long-lived benchmarks evolve through relabeling campaigns, errata, and papers' preprocessing choices; the same class name can denote drifting pixel sets across versions, corrupting longitudinal comparisons that the field reads as progress.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: diffing dataset versions and reconstructing papers' actual evaluation pixel-sets will reveal class-definition drift large enough to explain measurable fractions of reported multi-year 'progress' on affected classes, and papers citing the same benchmark differ silently in effective test sets (preprocessing forks) at a rate that makes a subset of published comparisons non-comparable - the field lacks semantic versioning and pays for it in phantom progress.
why_important: Longitudinal progress claims are the field's self-narrative; auditing their consistency is basic metrology.
why_possibly_novel: Version-drift accounting for segmentation benchmarks is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Diff Cityscapes/ADE versions and 20 papers' preprocessing forks, recompute a fixed model's score under each effective test set, tabulate the spread.
main_risk: Reconstructing papers' exact pipelines is laborious; prioritize the most-cited comparison chains.

one_liner: Effective headroom estimation: how much of each benchmark's remaining error is model-fixable versus reference noise - the saturation audit.
problem: Benchmarks near saturation reward noise-fitting, but the field lacks a standard estimate of each benchmark's effective headroom (remaining error that a correct model could actually reduce), so effort allocation across benchmarks is blind.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: decomposing residual error on major benchmarks (via multi-annotation, model consensus, and ambiguity measurement) will show several popular benchmarks have effective headroom below 2 points (further gains are style-fitting), while others retain large real headroom concentrated in specific classes - and publishing per-benchmark headroom would measurably shift where new methods report results (a testable sociological prediction).
why_important: Effort follows benchmarks; headroom accounting redirects the field's marginal week of work toward real problems.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic headroom estimation across dense benchmarks is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Apply the decomposition to 6 benchmarks using existing multi-annotation where available plus targeted re-annotation, publish headroom table.
main_risk: Headroom estimates depend on ambiguity modeling assumptions; report ranges under stated models.

one_liner: Within-benchmark duplication inflates scores: near-duplicate test images act as multipliers on style-matched models.
problem: Test sets assembled from web sources contain internal near-duplicates (same scene, same event, burst shots); metrics implicitly weight duplicated content multiply, favoring models that happen to fit the duplicated styles - the duplication structure of dense benchmarks is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: near-duplicate clustering of major test sets will find measurable duplication (several percent of images with intra-set near-dups), deduplicated re-scoring changes method rankings in close comparisons, and duplication is topic-biased (certain scene types over-weighted), meaning current scores encode hidden topical weightings nobody chose deliberately.
why_important: A cheap, definitive hygiene audit; close SOTA races are exactly where duplicate-weighting artifacts decide outcomes.
why_possibly_novel: Intra-benchmark duplication analysis for dense tasks is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Run embedding-based near-dup clustering on 5 test sets, re-score public models deduplicated, report rank sensitivity.
main_risk: Near-dup thresholds are judgment calls; report across threshold sweeps.

one_liner: Segmentation performance by geography of image origin: dense prediction has an unmeasured global-equity profile.
problem: KNOWN: object recognition performs worse on images from lower-income regions (Facebook's Dollar Street analyses). For segmentation - where infrastructure, vehicles, and household objects differ even more visually - the geographic performance profile has not been measured, though these models deploy globally.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: mainstream segmentation models show substantial performance gradients across image-origin geography (worse boundary AND recognition quality in under-represented regions), the gradient persists for supposedly universal classes (person, food, bed) not just region-specific ones, and gradient magnitude correlates with training-corpus geo-distribution estimates - making the data-origin ledger an actionable fairness instrument for dense prediction.
why_important: Segmentation increasingly gates real services (medical triage, agricultural tools, AR); an unmeasured geographic performance cliff is an equity failure waiting to surface.
why_possibly_novel: Geographic stratification of dense-prediction quality is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Annotate geo-diverse image samples (Dollar-Street-style) with masks, evaluate model zoo, regress performance on region and corpus-representation estimates.
main_risk: Annotation quality must be uniform across regions to avoid reproducing the artifact under audit; use one centralized expert team.

one_liner: The sensor gap: benchmarks are smartphone/DSLR photos, deployments are industrial/scientific sensors - quantify the unbenchmarked capture-hardware shift.
problem: Public benchmarks overwhelmingly sample consumer camera output (processed, sharpened, tone-mapped), while deployments run on machine-vision cameras, line-scan sensors, and scientific detectors with alien noise/optics profiles - a capture-hardware distribution gap that no benchmark measures.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: models transferred from consumer-photo training to industrial-sensor imagery degrade substantially even for identical scene content (verifiable with dual-capture rigs: consumer + machine-vision camera imaging the same scenes), the degradation localizes to texture- and noise-sensitive classes, and simple sensor-simulation augmentation (noise/optics models) recovers a large fraction - the gap is real, measurable, and cheaply mitigable once acknowledged.
why_important: Industrial vision is a huge deployment share served by benchmarks that never sampled its input distribution; the dual-capture measurement would ground years of anecdotal complaints.
why_possibly_novel: Dual-capture sensor-gap quantification is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Build dual-camera rig, capture 300 matched scenes, evaluate models cross-sensor, test sensor-simulation recovery.
main_risk: One industrial camera does not represent all; use 3 sensor types to bound diversity.

one_liner: PQ's 0.5-IoU matching cliff makes panoptic rankings noise-sensitive: measure how many published gaps live at the threshold.
problem: Panoptic Quality matches predictions to GT at a hard IoU>0.5 threshold; instances near the threshold flip between matched and unmatched under tiny changes, injecting discontinuous noise into scores - the fraction of published PQ differences attributable to near-threshold instances is unknown.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: perturbation analysis (jittering predictions/GT within annotation noise) shows PQ variance is dominated by near-threshold instances, a smooth-matching variant (soft credit around the threshold) reduces ranking noise substantially while preserving interpretation, and re-scoring recent panoptic literature with the smooth variant erases a measurable fraction of published gaps - the metric's discontinuity has been manufacturing significance.
why_important: Metric-induced noise wastes the field's effort ratifying phantom differences; a validated smooth variant is a drop-in repair.
why_possibly_novel: Threshold-cliff noise accounting for PQ is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Jitter-based variance decomposition of PQ on COCO-panoptic across models, implement smooth matching, re-score and compare rank stability.
main_risk: Any new metric fights adoption inertia; position as diagnostic first, replacement second.

one_liner: Longitudinal val-test gap growth: leaderboards teach the community to overfit validation sets - measure the ecosystem-level adaptive overfitting rate.
problem: KNOWN: adaptive overfitting on reused test sets was studied for classification (Recht et al. line of work) with reassuring results - but segmentation's smaller, older, more-reused validation sets and richer hyperparameter surfaces may behave worse, and nobody has run the equivalent audit for dense prediction.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: reproducing the fresh-test-set methodology for segmentation (new Cityscapes/ADE-protocol test images collected today) will show larger val-to-fresh performance drops for recent methods than early ones (growing adaptive overfitting), with the growth concentrated in methods using validation-heavy development (NAS, heavy tuning) - dense prediction's reassurance on this question is currently borrowed from classification without evidence.
why_important: If the drop grows with method recency, recent SOTA gains partly measure validation-set adaptation - the most fundamental audit a benchmark ecosystem can run on itself.
why_possibly_novel: Fresh-test-set replication for dense benchmarks is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Collect and annotate protocol-faithful fresh test sets (500 images) for 2 benchmarks, evaluate the historical model zoo, plot drop vs publication year.
main_risk: Fresh collection can accidentally shift distribution; protocol fidelity (same cities, seasons, cameras where possible) is the crux.

one_liner: Difficulty drift: modern models find different images hard than old models did - curated 'hard subsets' expire and need versioning.
problem: Curated hard-example subsets (built from some era's model failures) are used as fixed difficulty benchmarks, but difficulty is model-relative; whether old hard subsets remain hard - and whether difficulty ORDER is stable across model generations - determines their continued validity.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: per-image difficulty rankings correlate only moderately across model generations (difficulty drift is substantial), hard subsets curated pre-foundation-era are disproportionately solved by modern models (their hardness encoded era-specific weaknesses, not intrinsic difficulty), and a stable 'intrinsically hard' core (hard for ALL generations) exists and is characterizable - separating timeless difficulty (ambiguity, information limits) from era difficulty (fixable gaps).
why_important: Hard-subset benchmarks steer robustness research; expired hardness wastes effort and understates progress, while the intrinsic-core characterization is a durable scientific object.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-generation difficulty-drift measurement is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Evaluate model-zoo generations on fixed benchmarks, compute cross-era difficulty correlations, characterize the all-era-hard core.
main_risk: Generation boundaries are fuzzy; define by training-data era and capability cohorts.

one_liner: Masks reveal their dataset: annotation-style leakage is strong enough to classify a mask's source benchmark from geometry alone.
problem: If mask geometry alone (no image) identifies the source dataset with high accuracy, then dataset-specific annotation style is a large learnable signal - and cross-dataset evaluation partially tests style transfer rather than visual capability. The magnitude of style leakage has never been measured ecosystem-wide.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a geometry-only classifier distinguishes masks from 8 major datasets well above chance (style signatures are strong), models trained on each dataset reproduce its signature on NEW images (style is learned, not content-driven), and regressing cross-dataset performance drops on style distance shows style explains a substantial share of measured 'domain gaps' between datasets with similar imagery - the ecosystem's labels are dialects, and models learn the dialect.
why_important: Dialect effects contaminate every cross-dataset conclusion; measuring them enables style-normalized evaluation, a cleaner science.
why_possibly_novel: Ecosystem-wide style-leakage quantification is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Train mask-geometry dataset classifier, verify signature reproduction in model outputs, decompose cross-dataset gaps into style vs content components.
main_risk: Content differences (different class geometries per dataset) confound style; control by comparing within shared classes at matched size.

one_liner: Statistical power audit of segmentation SOTA claims: how many published gains survive bootstrap significance testing on their own benchmarks?
problem: Segmentation papers claim SOTA on point estimates over test sets with unquantified variance (image sampling, seed variance, near-threshold instances); the fraction of published gains that are statistically distinguishable from noise has never been computed for the field.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: applying image-level bootstrap plus seed-variance accounting to recent top-venue segmentation comparisons will show a substantial fraction (>30%) of claimed improvements are within noise (not significant at reasonable levels), non-significant gains concentrate in small-benchmark and small-delta papers, and the field's effective discovery rate is far lower than its publication rate implies - a meta-scientific measurement with direct norms-changing potential (report CIs, multiple seeds).
why_important: Publication-level noise pollutes meta-decisions (what directions 'work'); quantifying it is the prerequisite for fixing incentive structures.
why_possibly_novel: Field-wide significance auditing for dense prediction is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search (similar audits exist in other ML subfields - KNOWN pattern, e.g. metric-learning reality checks).
minimal_experiment: Reproduce 20 recent comparisons from public checkpoints, bootstrap test-set CIs and seed spread, tabulate survival rates.
main_risk: Reproduction burden; restrict to papers with released models to stay feasible.

one_liner: Video benchmarks annotate the easy frames: keyframe selection bias means reported VOS accuracy skips blur, transitions, and bad light.
problem: Video annotation pipelines select frames for labeling where annotation is feasible (sharp, well-lit, unambiguous), so evaluation systematically avoids the frames where models most likely fail - a sampling bias baked into every video benchmark's reported number.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: annotated frames in major video benchmarks differ measurably from unannotated neighbors (sharper, better-exposed, less motion - quantifiable via image statistics), model performance on pseudo-evaluable hard frames (via high-confidence temporal interpolation of GT) is substantially lower than reported numbers, and the bias grows with scene dynamism - published VOS scores are upper bounds with a measurable optimism gap.
why_important: Deployment consumes every frame, not curated ones; the optimism gap is exactly the deployment surprise waiting in video products.
why_possibly_novel: Annotated-frame selection-bias measurement for video benchmarks is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Compare image statistics of annotated vs neighboring frames across 4 VOS benchmarks, construct interpolation-based hard-frame evaluation, measure the gap.
main_risk: Interpolated GT on hard frames is imperfect; use conservative confidence gating and human spot checks.

one_liner: Patient-level leakage in public medical segmentation datasets: audit how many benchmarks let the same patient into train and test.
problem: Medical volumes from one patient (multiple slices, studies, or visits) appearing across train/test splits inflate performance via patient-specific memorization (anatomy, implants, scanner metadata burned into pixels); the prevalence of this leakage across public medical segmentation benchmarks is unaudited.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: patient-identity forensics (anatomical fingerprint matching across split boundaries) will find leakage in a meaningful fraction of public medical segmentation datasets (especially aggregated/multi-source ones), leakage-affected benchmarks show measurably inflated scores (re-split evaluation drops performance), and the inflation is largest for high-capacity models - a hygiene audit with direct clinical-claims consequences.
why_important: Medical performance claims feed regulatory and clinical decisions; patient leakage is the most consequential form of benchmark inflation in this domain.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-dataset patient-leakage forensics at ecosystem scale is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search (individual dataset issues are occasionally reported - KNOWN pattern).
minimal_experiment: Build anatomical-fingerprint matcher (bone structure, vessel trees), scan 10 public datasets' splits, re-split and re-evaluate where leakage is found.
main_risk: Fingerprint false positives (similar anatomy) must be controlled; validate matcher on datasets with known patient IDs.

one_liner: Negative-set poverty in safety datasets: smoke/fire benchmarks lack the hard negatives (fog, steam, sunsets) that dominate deployment false alarms.
problem: Detection benchmarks report false-positive rates against their own negative sets, but safety datasets' negatives are conveniences (random frames), not the confusable phenomena that cause real false alarms - so reported FPRs bear no relation to deployed FPRs, in an unquantified way.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: constructing a hard-negative bank (fog banks, steam vents, dust, sunsets, orange lighting, reflective surfaces) and re-evaluating public smoke/fire models will show deployment-realistic FPRs orders of magnitude above benchmark FPRs, model rankings will reorder substantially (benchmark-FPR optimization does not transfer), and the hard-negative bank composition needed to PREDICT deployed FPR is discoverable from false-alarm logs - benchmark negatives need engineering as much as positives.
why_important: False alarms determine whether safety systems get trusted or unplugged; benchmark-to-deployment FPR translation is the missing number for the whole application class.
why_possibly_novel: Hard-negative-bank methodology with deployment-FPR validation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Assemble hard-negative video bank, re-evaluate 6 public models, compare with any obtainable deployment false-alarm statistics.
main_risk: Deployment FPR data is proprietary; partner with one camera-network operator or use public wildfire-camera archives.

one_liner: Turntable bias in transparent-object datasets: background diversity deficit makes lab-collected benchmarks trivially solvable by background memorization.
problem: Transparent/reflective object datasets are heavily lab-collected (turntables, repeated backgrounds); models may key on the small background vocabulary rather than object evidence, making benchmark scores unrepresentative - the background-diversity deficit and its exploitation are unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: background-swap evaluation (same objects composited onto novel backgrounds) collapses transparent-object SOTA disproportionately compared to opaque-object controls (transparency models are more background-dependent by necessity - but current ones are background-MEMORIZING, a different thing), and per-dataset background vocabulary size predicts the collapse magnitude - turning an intuition about lab bias into a measured validity criterion for the whole dataset family.
why_important: Transparent-object perception feeds robotics safety; validity criteria for its benchmarks protect against false confidence.
why_possibly_novel: Background-vocabulary auditing for transparency datasets is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Quantify background diversity across 5 transparency datasets, run background-swap collapse tests on public models with opaque controls.
main_risk: Compositing transparent objects onto new backgrounds is technically hard (refraction must be re-rendered); use capture-based swaps where possible.

one_liner: Aesthetic bias: benchmarks oversample well-composed photographs, and performance correlates with photographic quality - ugly images are the real test.
problem: Dataset images pass through human selection filters (what people photograph, upload, and curators keep) biased toward aesthetic composition; deployment sees uncomposed frames (fixed cameras, robots, egocentric streams). Whether model performance secretly tracks aesthetic quality has not been measured.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: per-image segmentation performance correlates measurably with aesthetics scores (composition, exposure) even controlling for content difficulty, benchmarks' aesthetics distributions sit far above deployment-stream distributions (quantifiable gap), and reweighting evaluation toward deployment-realistic aesthetics drops scores and reorders methods - the ecosystem has been grading models on portfolio shots while deploying them on security-camera reality.
why_important: A quantified aesthetics-performance coupling would explain systematic deployment disappointments and motivate uncomposed-image benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Aesthetics-stratified performance analysis is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Score benchmark and deployment-stream images with aesthetics models, measure performance-aesthetics correlation with content-difficulty controls, construct reweighted evaluation.
main_risk: Aesthetics scores entangle with genuine difficulty (blur IS harder); careful covariate design is the whole game.

one_liner: Annotation-display resolution is missing metadata: masks were drawn at unknown zoom levels, making boundary precision claims unanchorable.
problem: A mask's boundary precision is bounded by the resolution at which the annotator VIEWED the image, but datasets never record display/zoom conditions - so boundary supervision quality varies invisibly within and across datasets, and evaluation cannot distinguish model error from annotation-viewing artifacts.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: viewing-resolution signatures are forensically recoverable from mask geometry (quantization patterns, minimum feature sizes reveal the annotation zoom), datasets show wide internal variance in recovered viewing resolution, and boundary-metric noise correlates with recovered viewing resolution - establishing display metadata as a required annotation-protocol field and providing retroactive quality stratification for existing data.
why_important: An entire hidden quality dimension of every existing dataset becomes measurable, enabling resolution-stratified training and honest boundary evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: Viewing-resolution forensics for annotations is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Validate the forensic estimator on controlled-zoom annotations, apply to major datasets, correlate recovered resolution with boundary-noise estimates.
main_risk: Forensic recovery may be too noisy per-mask; dataset-level distributions may be the honest granularity.

one_liner: Intra-dataset ontology noise: the same dataset labels identical object types inconsistently, and the confusion structure is measurable and learnable-around.
problem: Within one dataset, borderline objects (armchair vs chair, path vs road, shrub vs tree) are labeled inconsistently across images by different annotators - intra-dataset ontology noise that models must absorb, distinct from inter-dataset convention differences and never separately quantified.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: intra-dataset labeling of borderline categories is inconsistent at measurable rates (findable via visually-near-duplicate object pairs with different labels within one dataset), models resolve the inconsistency by learning context-dependent arbitrary rules (probeable), and class-merging evaluation (scoring confusable-pair classes jointly) recovers substantial apparent performance - separating true recognition failure from ontology noise absorption in every dataset's confusion matrix.
why_important: Confusion-matrix entries between sibling classes drive per-class conclusions and long-tail claims; knowing which entries are ontology noise re-reads much of that literature.
why_possibly_novel: Within-dataset ontology-noise quantification via near-duplicate label disagreement is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Mine visually-similar object pairs with conflicting labels within ADE/COCO, estimate per-class-pair inconsistency rates, re-evaluate models under class-merged protocols.
main_risk: Visual similarity does not guarantee same true class; human adjudication of mined pairs needed.

one_liner: LVIS federated annotation makes rare-class scores statistically fragile: put confidence intervals on every rare-class claim.
problem: Federated annotation (KNOWN: LVIS design - not every image checked for every class) means rare-class evaluation rests on few positives and unverified negatives; the resulting statistical fragility of rare-class AP - and how many published rare-class gains fall inside it - has not been systematically computed.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: bootstrap confidence intervals on LVIS rare-class metrics are wide enough to contain most published method-to-method rare-class improvements (the celebrated gains are statistically unresolvable), the unverified-negative assumption injects additional bias measurable via exhaustive re-annotation of an image sample, and rare-class conclusions require aggregation protocols (class grouping, hierarchical models) the field does not use - current rare-class science runs below its own noise floor.
why_important: Long-tail methods are ranked by exactly these fragile numbers; the field needs to know which of its conclusions the data can actually support.
why_possibly_novel: Fragility quantification of federated rare-class evaluation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Bootstrap LVIS rare-class metrics across published models, exhaustively re-annotate 500 images to measure the negative-assumption bias, overlay published deltas on CIs.
main_risk: None serious - this is careful statistics on existing artifacts; main cost is the re-annotation sample.

one_liner: Same dataset, different numbers: meta-analysis of score spread for identical model-benchmark pairs across papers reveals the reproduction noise floor.
problem: The same model evaluated on the same benchmark yields different numbers across papers (preprocessing, resolution, checkpoint, protocol forks); this reproduction spread - the ecosystem's effective measurement noise - has never been compiled, though it bounds what score differences can mean.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: compiling reported scores for identical model-benchmark pairs across 100+ papers will show reproduction spreads (often 1-3 points) comparable to typical claimed improvements, spread correlates with protocol under-specification per benchmark (some benchmarks are reproducible, others are not), and the analysis yields a reproduction-noise table that any reviewer can use to sanity-check claimed gains - the field's measurement infrastructure quantified from its own literature, no new experiments needed.
why_important: The cheapest possible meta-audit (literature mining only) that would immediately recalibrate how everyone reads improvement claims.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-paper reproduction-spread compilation for segmentation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Mine reported baseline numbers from open-access papers for 10 model-benchmark pairs, tabulate spreads, correlate with protocol specification completeness.
main_risk: Papers may cite each other's numbers (spread underestimated); track citation provenance of each number.

one_liner: Measure human mIoU: segmentation benchmarks lack the human-performance baselines that every claims discussion needs.
problem: Unlike ImageNet classification (KNOWN: human baselines exist), segmentation benchmarks have no measured human performance under the benchmark's own protocol - so 'superhuman' or 'approaching human' claims float free of data, and the human-model error comparison (WHERE they differ) has no reference.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: careful human evaluation under benchmark protocols will show humans BELOW current SOTA on consistency-demanding aspects (class-boundary conventions, per-pixel diligence over large stuff regions) but far ABOVE on ambiguity resolution and rare-object recognition - a crossing profile, not a single number - and human-vs-model error decorrelation identifies exactly the residual capabilities models lack, sharpening what 'progress toward human-level segmentation' should even mean.
why_important: Reference points anchor a field's self-assessment; segmentation has been running without one for fifteen years.
why_possibly_novel: Protocol-faithful human baselines for standard segmentation benchmarks are UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Run trained human annotators through Cityscapes/ADE evaluation subsets under time-controlled conditions, score identically to models, publish the profile.
main_risk: Human performance depends heavily on time budget and training; report as curves over effort, not points.

one_liner: Model-in-the-loop adversarial test collection for segmentation: does human-sourced hardness transfer across models or just defeat the collection-time model?
problem: Adversarial benchmark collection (humans search for model failures, Dynabench-style - KNOWN in NLP/classification) has not been seriously run for segmentation, and its core validity question - whether collected hardness is model-specific or generalizes - is open for dense tasks where failure modes are more structured.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: human-in-the-loop collection against one segmentation model yields examples that transfer as hard to unrelated models at high rates for certain failure families (ambiguous boundaries, rare configurations - shared data holes) but not others (model-specific texture quirks), and the transferable/non-transferable split aligns with the shared-blind-spot decomposition - making adversarial collection a practical shared-hole prospecting tool, with known limits, for dense prediction.
why_important: If hardness transfers, adversarial collection becomes the cheapest way to find the ecosystem's real gaps; if not, a popular methodology is invalid for dense tasks - either answer matters.
why_possibly_novel: Transfer-validity analysis of adversarial collection for segmentation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Run collection sessions against one public model (annotators photograph/find failure scenes), evaluate collected set on 8 other models, decompose transfer by failure family.
main_risk: Collector creativity bounds what is found; use diverse collector pools and seed taxonomies.

one_liner: The ignore-region census: what fraction of each benchmark's pixels are excluded from evaluation, what lives there, and who benefits?
problem: Benchmarks exclude void/ignore/ambiguous pixels from scoring at rates nobody tabulates; the excluded content is non-random (crowds, boundaries, distant clutter - often the hardest content), so exclusion rates and composition silently shape what benchmarks measure and which methods look good.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a census across 10 benchmarks will show ignore fractions varying widely (2-20%) with systematically hard content over-represented in exclusions, models disagree most exactly there (confirming difficulty), and hypothetically scoring ignore regions with best-effort reference labels would reorder methods (some methods' advantages evaporate outside the scored region) - exclusion policy is an unacknowledged benchmark design choice with ranking consequences, deserving explicit reporting standards.
why_important: What benchmarks refuse to measure defines them as much as what they measure; the census makes an invisible design choice visible and comparable.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-benchmark ignore-region census is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Tabulate ignore statistics and content composition across benchmarks, obtain best-effort labels for samples of ignored regions, measure model disagreement and ranking sensitivity.
main_risk: Best-effort labels in ignored regions are noisy by construction (that is why they were ignored); use consensus protocols and report uncertainty.
